title: Coloured swirl mirror glaze
subtitle: multi-colour marble and galaxy mirror glaze effect
excerpt: A coloured swirl mirror glaze uses multiple tinted pours of gelatine-set glaze over a frozen entremet to produce a fluid marble or galaxy pattern on the surface. The colours blend where they meet on the cake but don't fully mix, each retains its identity in the swirl. Getting this right depends entirely on glaze temperature, frozen cake temperature, and the order of pours.
sourceNotes: Mirror glaze (glacage miroir in French) is a gelatine-based glaze made with condensed milk, glucose, sugar, and chocolate, heated and then cooled to working temperature before being poured over a frozen entremet. The technique has origins in French haute pâtisserie and was adapted for the multi-colour swirl format in the early 2010s, when 'galaxy cake' and 'marble glaze' videos spread rapidly on social media. The key technical parameter, glaze temperature of 32,35°C, was documented in professional pâtisserie training well before the social media trend and remains unchanged.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The glaze can be made up to 3 days ahead, stored in the fridge, and reheated gently to working temperature.
recipe.temperatureNote: glaze working temperature; too hot = slides off, too cold = sets before it flows

content.text: A coloured swirl mirror glaze requires a frozen entremet, multiple batches of glaze tinted to different colours, and precise temperature control. The glaze must be poured at 32,35°C, warm enough to flow, cool enough not to melt the frozen cake surface and run off. Get the temperature right and the swirl effect appears as the colours meet and bleed into each other on the curved surface.

items.prepNote: platinum grade, soaked in cold water

content.text: Soak the gelatine leaves in cold water for 5 minutes until soft. In a saucepan combine the sugar, glucose, and water. Bring to the boil, stirring, and cook for 1 minute. Pour over the chopped white chocolate and condensed milk in a tall jug. Squeeze out the gelatine and add to the jug. Leave for 2 minutes, then blend with a stick blender until completely smooth and glossy. Keep the blender submerged to avoid bubbles. Strain through a fine sieve. Divide the glaze between three jugs. Colour each a different shade with oil-based food colouring, oil-based colours integrate without breaking the emulsion. Leave to cool, stirring occasionally, until each jug reaches 32,35°C on a probe thermometer.
Prepare the frozen cake and glazing setup

The entremet must be frozen solid, at least 8 hours. Remove from the freezer and unmould onto a wire rack set over a deep-sided tray to catch the drips. Work quickly once the cake is out of the freezer; condensation will begin forming on the surface within a few minutes, and water droplets cause the glaze to crater.

All three glazes must be at 32,35°C simultaneously. Pour the darkest colour over the cake first, starting from the centre and letting it flow to the edges. Immediately pour the second colour in a thin stream in a circular motion around the top, then the third in a tighter spiral toward the centre. The colours will bleed into each other as they flow down the sides. Do not touch or spread the glaze once poured, any intervention leaves marks. Leave on the rack for 5 minutes until the drips slow, then trim drips from the base with a small knife and transfer to a serving plate.
